questions: Ask your partner to send the exact remote-work policy to their HR and ask in writing: may they work from Switzerland, and who handles Swiss tax, social insurance and registration for them?
Can you get the subteam lead role, its scope and a rough timeline written into the offer letter or a signed side letter, and what does the hiring manager say when you ask?

Ask the hiring manager directly (not the recruiter) about the planned headcount, the funding situation and whether any reorganization or hiring freeze is under discussion; what do they say, and does it match what you find on LinkedIn about recent departures and layoffs?
Read the contract's probation clause: how long is the probation, what notice period applies to each side, and what severance, if any, applies if you are let go in the first six months?

Take three real flat listings in the Zurich areas you could accept and add up actual rent, deposit and commute; how long are viewings taking according to agents or local housing groups, and what would temporary housing cost for three months?

Recalculate the 40% figure from your salary slip basis: subtract Swiss income tax, mandatory health insurance, and social contributions, and compare with your current net in Munich. What is the net difference per month?
Is the bonus or equity part of the offer contractually guaranteed, and how much of the 40% depends on it?
Talk to two or three people who currently work on the Zurich team, or recently left it: what do they say about workload, the promised growth, and how the manager handled earlier promises?
Ask your current employer, with the offer in hand or as a hypothetical, whether a senior or lead path exists within two years; what is the answer and in what form (written, from whom)?
Ask your partner separately what they need to be happy in Zurich (social contacts, language, office or co-working access), and have them spend a week there working remotely before you sign.

lean.option: Accept the Zurich offer and move
lean.reasons: The offer pays about 40% more after cost of living, promises a step up with a subteam lead role within a year, the partner can work remotely from Zurich, and the Munich job has no senior opening in sight.

premortem: The reorganization at the Zurich company, already in discussion, cancels the new subteam; the hiring manager leaves within six months and the promised lead role disappears, leaving a senior title with no added responsibility.

The probation period and Swiss contract terms are shorter on notice than expected, and the company lets the person go during a hiring freeze after three months, when they have already signed a lease and moved.

The partner's employer allows remote work only in Germany for tax or legal reasons; working from Switzerland triggers social security and permit issues, so the employer withdraws permission and the partner must quit or return.
The cost-of-living adjustment underestimated housing: finding a flat takes months in a tight market, temporary housing eats savings, and the real net advantage is half what was estimated.

The partner is isolated working from home in a new country with no network and little German-speaking social life, and the relationship strain from the move, not the job, becomes the main reason they return to Munich after a year.

beliefs.belief: The Zurich offer is worth about 40% more after living costs.
beliefs.rests_on: A personal comparison using general cost-of-living figures and the offered salary.
beliefs.how_wrong: It may omit Swiss taxes, health insurance, deposits, childcare or commuting, and housing costs may differ from averages; the bonus or equity may not be guaranteed.

beliefs.belief: The hiring manager will really give them a subteam lead role within a year.
beliefs.rests_on: What the recruiter said and the hiring manager's verbal wish.
beliefs.how_wrong: It is a spoken statement, partly relayed by a recruiter, not written in the contract, and depends on growth, budget and the manager staying.

beliefs.belief: The team is growing and the company is stable.
beliefs.how_wrong: Recruiters have an interest in presenting the company positively; actual headcount plans, funding and recent layoffs have not been verified.

beliefs.belief: The partner can keep their job from Zurich.
beliefs.rests_on: The partner's employer's general remote work policy.
beliefs.how_wrong: Policy may cover only certain countries, and working from Switzerland may raise tax, social insurance and employer registration issues that were not checked with HR.

beliefs.belief: Staying in Munich offers no path to a senior role.
beliefs.rests_on: The absence of an opening and the person's impression of the company.
beliefs.how_wrong: Openings can appear unexpectedly, and the employer may react to a competing offer with a promotion; this was not tested by asking.

beliefs.belief: The partner and they will be happy living in Zurich.
beliefs.rests_on: A general expectation based on visits or reputation.
beliefs.how_wrong: Short visits differ from daily life, and the partner's social needs and the language and housing situation have not been tried.

beliefs.belief: Ten days and three months are enough to decide and to relocate properly.
beliefs.how_wrong: Housing search, permits, registration and notice in the current job may take longer than assumed, and the timeline has not been checked with the employer.
